flashcards.q: State the general formula for usable hosts given a prefix length, and the one exception.
flashcards.a: usable hosts = 2^(32-prefix) - 2 (subtract network and broadcast addresses). Exception: /31 (RFC 3021), used for point-to-point links -- both addresses are usable, no broadcast exists.
/24 = 256 addresses, 254 usable. /27 = 32 addresses, 30 usable, block size 32. /22 = 1024 addresses, 1022 usable, spans four /24s.

flashcards.q: What is the block-size shortcut for fast subnet math?
flashcards.a: 256 minus the mask's last nonzero octet value = block size. E.g. mask 255.255.255.224 -> 256-224=32.

flashcards.q: State the routing rule for resolving multiple matching routes to the same destination.
flashcards.a: Longest prefix match always wins -- the most specific matching route is chosen, regardless of insertion order; ties on equal prefix length are broken by administrative distance then metric.

flashcards.q: What mechanism lets IPv4 avoid in-network fragmentation, and what ICMP message drives it?
flashcards.a: Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD, RFC 1191): sender sets DF; if a router can't forward without fragmenting, it drops the packet and returns ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed and DF Set) with the next-hop MTU.

flashcards.q: Describe the PMTUD black hole failure and its observable symptom.
flashcards.a: A firewall blocks the ICMP 'frag needed' message, so the sender never learns to shrink packets. Symptom: TCP handshake and small requests work fine, but any payload crossing the MTU threshold hangs -- tcpdump shows a large packet leaving with no ACK and no ICMP response, retransmitted repeatedly until timeout.

flashcards.q: Give the four MTU numbers to know cold.
flashcards.a: Standard Ethernet 1500. PPPoE 1492 (8B PPPoE header). Jumbo frames 9000 (sometimes 9216). IPv6 minimum guaranteed 1280.

SNAT rewrites source address (outbound sharing). DNAT rewrites destination address (port-forward/LB). PAT/NAPT = SNAT + port rewrite, the mechanism that lets many hosts share one public IP, tracked by a state table keyed on the 4-tuple.

flashcards.q: What two categories of things break under NAT, and why?
flashcards.a: 1) Unsolicited inbound connections -- no state-table entry exists for a connection nobody inside initiated. 2) Protocols embedding IPs/ports in their payload (FTP active mode, SIP/SDP) -- NAT only rewrites headers, not application data, unless an ALG or STUN/TURN/ICE fixes the embedded address.

flashcards.q: List the concrete differences between IPv4 and IPv6 that matter in production.
flashcards.a: 32-bit (~4.3B, exhausted 2011) vs 128-bit (~3.4e38). ARP (broadcast) vs NDP (ICMPv6 multicast). Router fragmentation allowed vs never (host-only, ICMPv6 Packet Too Big). 20-60B variable header vs 40B fixed. IPv4 has a header checksum recomputed every hop; IPv6 removed it entirely, relying on L2/L4 checksums.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't IPv6 allow routers to fragment packets?
flashcards.a: Deliberate design: fragmentation cost is pushed entirely to the originating host (via an IPv6 Fragment extension header added only by the sender); routers that get an oversized packet just drop it and send ICMPv6 Packet Too Big -- PMTUD is mandatory, not optional, with no in-network fallback.

flashcards.q: What's the standard mitigation for a PMTUD black hole when you can't guarantee ICMP passes through?
flashcards.a: TCP MSS clamping at the border router/firewall -- rewrite the MSS option in SYN packets so TCP never tries to send a segment that would need fragmentation on that path.
